description.content:
The HTTP contract of the Trove core service. Four rules run through all of it.

**The envelope.** Every route below answers with
`ApiResponse{success, data, error, meta}`. A success is `{"success": true}`
plus `data` when the operation returns a value (`data` is *omitted*, not
null, when it returns none — Jackson serialises the envelope with
`@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)`). A failure is `{"success": false, "error": {…}}`
with no `data`. `meta` carries pagination and is absent on every operation
in this version. The single exception to the envelope in the whole API is
`GET /v1/status`, which is bare so an uptime probe has something trivial to
key off.

**Auth modes.** One session, two carriers, chosen per request with
`X-Trove-Auth-Mode`. In **bearer** mode (the default when the header is
absent, and what the mobile client uses) the tokens come back in the
response body and the caller sends `Authorization: Bearer …`. In **cookie**
mode (`X-Trove-Auth-Mode: cookie`, what the web client sends) the body
carries no tokens at all and the server sets `__Host-trove_access` and
`__Host-trove_refresh` — HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/. Because
the two modes return different shapes, every session-bearing response is a
`oneOf` and the client discriminates on which fields are present.

**CSRF.** Demanded only of requests that carry an ambient browser
credential — but the two demands are separate rules with different
triggers, and a client that conflates them will send a header the server
never asked for or, worse, expect one it does not get.

* The **double-submit token** (`X-XSRF-TOKEN`, echoing the non-HttpOnly
  `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie the server plants) is demanded of any mutating
  request that either presents a session cookie or declares
  `X-Trove-Auth-Mode: cookie` — *including the browser's anonymous login
  and register*, because login CSRF, logging a victim into the attacker's
  account, is a real attack and only the token stops it.
* **`X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`** is demanded only once a request
  has actually authenticated **through the session cookie**. An anonymous
  cookie-mode login or register has no session to ride and does not need
  it, though the web client sends it on everything anyway.

A bearer caller sends neither and is never checked — a third-party page
cannot set an `Authorization` header, so there is nothing to ride. A
missing token is 403 `forbidden`; a missing `X-Requested-With` on a
cookie-authenticated mutation is 403 `csrf-header-missing`.

**Errors.** RFC 7807 inside the envelope:
`error{type, title, status, detail, instance, requestId, fieldErrors}`.
`type` is always `https://trove.finance/errors/<slug>` and the slug — not
the status, not the prose — is what clients switch on. `instance` is the
matched route template (`/api/v1/auth/invites/{token}`), never the caller's
raw URI. `requestId` is echoed in the `X-Request-Id` response header and is
the string to quote when reporting a 500. `fieldErrors` is present only on
a 400 that failed field validation, as `[{field, message}]`.

Requests that match no operation are answered outside this document:
an unknown path is 404 `not-found`, a known path with an unsupported method
is 405 `method-not-allowed`, and a body sent with an unsupported media type
currently falls through to 500 `internal-server-error`.

**Step-up.** The body carries the caller's current password and, where a
second factor is enrolled, a current code. A wrong one is 403
`step-up-required` and records a failed-login security event.

**A member who signs in only through an identity provider has no
password**, so the factor set is resolved from what the account actually
has: a member with a local password proves it (plus a code where TOTP is
enrolled); a member with no password but an enrolled second factor
proves the code alone; a member with neither is refused 403
`step-up-required` with an explanation, because there is nothing left to
prove and a session alone is exactly the credential this step-up exists
to distrust. The way forward for that member is an administrator-issued
password reset link, after which this route works.

**What deleting does.** The account is *soft* deleted: it is deactivated,
stamped with the moment of deletion, and every session of it is revoked
immediately, so the very next request with an existing token is refused.

liabilities, subscriptions and receipts, including the receipt images —

removed, because an incident review must not be erasable by deleting an

with the same address before the erasure has run answers 400

the instant the grace ends. A member who means to come back with the same
address should ask an administrator to restore the account instead.

from their timezone, not the server's. A second request the same day is

deliberately not expressed in the rate limiter, which buckets by path and

item.name: Remove a member of the household

description.content:
**Requires the `ADMIN` role.**

Two refusals, and the order matters. A member of another household — or
an id that does not exist — is **404**, not 403: the lookup is
household-scoped, so "not yours" and "does not exist" are the same answer
and neither confirms an id is real. The household's last `ADMIN` is
**409 `conflict`**: an install whose only administrator has been deleted
has no way back in, because registration is closed by default and both
invites and the settings flag are admin routes. The guard counts rather
than comparing ids, so self-deletion is allowed exactly while somebody
else can still administer the household, and it runs inside one
transaction behind a lock on the household row.

**This is a soft delete, and it is the same path `DELETE /v1/me` takes**
— one guard, one lock, one event, so the two cannot drift. The member is
deactivated and stamped rather than erased, and every session of theirs
is revoked immediately: sign-in, refresh, the weekly digest, insight
recipients and webhook audiences all exclude them from that instant. They
stay listed by `GET /v1/admin/users` with `active: false`, which is how
an administrator finds them again, and
`POST /v1/admin/users/{id}/restore` brings them back for a grace period
(seven days by default). Only after that does a scheduled job erase the

item.name: Upload a CSV or OFX file and preview what importing it would do

description.content:
(Required) The CSV, OFX or QFX file. Its declared content type must be
one this server accepts (`text/csv`, `text/plain`,
`application/csv`, `application/vnd.ms-excel`,
`application/x-ofx`, `application/x-qfx`, `application/ofx`
or `application/octet-stream`) **and** its first bytes must
match the format it claims to be.

it overrides the account the file's own `ACCTID` would
resolve to.

The two source kinds that come from a file. `SIMPLEFIN` is fetched over
the network and `MANUAL` is typed in, so neither has a file to batch —
which is also what the `import_batch.source_kind` CHECK says.

Stores the uploaded file, works out what is in it, and answers with a
**preview**. Nothing is written to the ledger by this operation — not one
transaction row. The batch is created with status `PREVIEW`; a separate
`POST /v1/imports/{id}/commit` is what inserts anything.

**The format is sniffed**, so `sourceKind` is optional: the first bytes
of the file decide whether it is OFX 1.x (SGML), OFX 2.x (XML) or CSV.
Sending `sourceKind` narrows the sniff rather than overriding it — a file
that is not what it claims to be is refused.

**`accountId` is required for CSV** and optional for OFX. A CSV file
carries no account identity at all, so the member has to say which
account the rows belong to. An OFX file carries `ACCTID`, and the server
looks that up as `(household, OFX, ACCTID)`: the same file uploaded twice
reuses the account it created the first time instead of making a second
one and duplicating every transaction on it.

**What the preview contains.** Counts of what committing would do — new
rows, exact duplicates, near-duplicates and rows that cannot be accepted
— the detected column mapping for a CSV, a small sample of parsed rows,
and, when the file's dates are ambiguous between `dd/MM/yyyy` and
`MM/dd/yyyy`, the **candidate formats with the sample values that make
them ambiguous**. The member picks one and sends it back on the commit;
the server never guesses silently between the two.

**The file and the account must be the same kind.** `POST /v1/accounts`
accepts `SIMPLEFIN`, `OFX`, `CSV` and `MANUAL`, and only an account of
the file's own kind can take an import: a CSV may be uploaded against a
`CSV` account and an OFX file against an `OFX` account. Anything else is
refused here, at upload, rather than being previewed and then failing at
commit — the commit resolves its parser from the account, so a mismatched
batch could never be committed and, because undo requires a committed
batch, could never be cleaned up either.

the container's multipart cap, the import's own per-file cap, or the
household's total allowance for uploads not yet committed or swept — the
last two checked against the declared part size before the body is read.
400 `validation-error` covers everything else the upload can be refused
for: a content type this operation does not accept, a file whose bytes
are not the format they claim to be, a zip or gzip wrapper, more rows
than the row cap allows, a CSV whose header cannot be mapped, a missing
`accountId` on a CSV, or an `accountId` naming an account of another
kind.

description.content:
One turn of a conversation with the member's own AI endpoint, over a
context block built from **their household's ledger**. Streaming or not,
decided by `stream`.

**Whose AI, and whose data.** The endpoint, the key and the timeouts are
the caller's own (`GET /v1/ai/settings`); the ledger figures are their
household's; the conversation is theirs alone. A household mate cannot
read, continue or clear it — the opposite of every ledger route, and the
reason a session id that belongs to somebody else is 404 rather than 403.

**Sessions.** `X-Session-Id` is set on **every** response, streaming or
not. Send it back to continue a conversation; omit it and a new one is
started and its id returned. The value is the conversation's own id —
there is no second correlation id to keep in step with it — and it is
not a session in the authentication sense: it carries no privileges, it
is not a refresh-token family, and presenting one that is not yours is
simply 404.

**`messages` is the turn you are sending, not the history.** The server
takes the **last** entry, which must be `role: user`, as the question,
and rebuilds the preceding turns from its own store for the named
session. Earlier entries in the array are ignored. That is deliberate:
accepting a client-supplied `assistant` turn would let a page put words
into the model's mouth and then quote them back as the coach's own.

**What is sent to the endpoint.** A system prompt, a context block, the
stored history window and this question. The context block carries
aggregates only — this month's spend, income and net in each currency
the household holds, the current budget period's envelope allocations
and spend by category name, asset and liability totals, and the
subscription run rate and flagged count. It carries no account number,
no access URL, no API key, no receipt image, no raw transaction row and
no other member's identity. A section whose read fails or overruns the
five-second deadline is stated as unavailable rather than reported as
zero.

Every coach payload is classified `SENSITIVE`, so a member whose
`privacyTier` is `CLOUD_OK` is refused with 403 `ai-policy-blocked`
before any connection is opened. `LOCAL_ONLY` is what this feature needs.

**The answer is text, and nothing else.** It is stored and displayed and
never interpreted: no tool calling, no function calling, no id, category,
URL or command is ever taken from it. Control characters are stripped and
the stored answer is capped.

### Streaming (`stream=true`)

`200` with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, written frame by frame as
the endpoint produces them — nothing buffers the body. The frames are
exactly:

```
data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Your "}}]}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"groceries "}}]}

data: [DONE]
```

and a failure **after** the stream has opened arrives in band, as the
last frame, with no `[DONE]` after it:

```
data: {"error":{"type":"https://trove.finance/errors/ai-timeout","title":"Gateway Timeout","status":504,"detail":"…","instance":"/api/v1/chat/completions","requestId":"…"}}
```

A stored answer is capped, and a stream that reaches the cap ends with an
in-band `answer-too-long` frame rather than `[DONE]`: what arrived is
kept and is on the screen, the endpoint did not fail, and the slug says
so. A saved endpoint that has stopped passing the egress policy ends the
stream the same way, with `outbound-url-rejected` — the same 400 the
non-streaming form answers.

The in-band error never carries a stack trace, the prompt, the endpoint's
host or the endpoint's own response body. A client reads `response.ok`
and the content type **before** treating a body as a stream: everything
that can be decided before the first byte — an unknown session, AI
switched off, the privacy tier, a malformed body, the rate limiter — is
an ordinary JSON `ApiResponse` with the usual status, and only after
those does the stream open. A partial answer whose stream then fails is
still persisted; the question is persisted before the call, so a dropped
connection loses the answer but never the question.

### Not streaming (`stream=false`, the default)

The ordinary envelope with the whole answer, and the endpoint failures as
real status codes (502 / 504) rather than as frames.

Receipt images and what the server can read off them. A receipt is
shared household ledger data: every member sees every receipt, and the
uploader is recorded on the row rather than being its scope.

The upload is hardened rather than trusted — declared size, magic bytes,
a header-only dimension probe, the household's storage quota, and a
re-encode to JPEG that strips EXIF by construction. Extraction is the
uploader's own vision model when they have configured one; when they
have not, which is every install by default, the image is stored and the
fields are the member's to fill in. That is the ordinary outcome, not a
failure.

description.content:
(Required) The receipt image. Declared content type must be
`image/jpeg` or `image/png`, and the first bytes must match
it.

How the image arrived. `UPLOAD` is a file the member chose, `SCAN` a
photograph taken in the app. Defaults to `UPLOAD` when absent.

The pre-collapse enum also had `EMAIL`; there is no email ingress in
this design, so a value nothing can produce is not in the contract.

Stores a receipt photograph and starts processing it. The answer is
**202** and carries `{id, status, createdAt}` and nothing else — not a
full receipt. That shape is stated deliberately: the row exists the
moment this returns, but the fields on it do not yet, and handing back
an almost-empty receipt would invite a client to render it. Poll
`GET /v1/receipts/{id}/status`, or fetch the whole row from
`GET /v1/receipts/{id}`.

**Only JPEG and PNG are accepted.** The declared content type must be
`image/jpeg` or `image/png` *and* the first bytes must agree with it.
HEIC is refused here on purpose — the mobile client converts before it
uploads — and PDF is not accepted in this version at all.

**The bytes that are stored are not the bytes that were sent.** Every
accepted image is re-encoded to JPEG at quality 85, at most 2000 px on
its long edge, and only that re-encoding is written to disk. The
original is never stored, which is what removes EXIF — the GPS
coordinates a phone camera writes into a receipt photograph included —
by construction rather than by a tag-stripping library that might miss
one. A consequence worth stating: the file this operation stores is
always `image/jpeg`, whatever was sent, and that is what
`GET /v1/receipts/{id}/download` serves back.

413 `upload-too-large` is one of three ceilings, all answering the same
slug because from a client's point of view there is one refusal: the
container's multipart cap, this operation's own per-file cap, and the
household's total receipt-storage quota. The last two are checked
against the part's **declared** size before its bytes are read, so a
client that is over either one is refused without the server decoding
anything. The quota is then re-checked exactly, against the size of the
re-encoded pair that is about to be written, because those bytes and not
the upload are what occupy the volume; that second check can only refuse
an upload the first one would also have refused.

400 `validation-error` covers everything else: an empty part, a content
type this operation does not accept, bytes that are not the format they
claim to be, an image whose header declares more pixels than the server
will decode, or an image that is not decodable at all. Nothing derived
from the uploaded filename ever reaches a path — the storage key is
generated server-side.

vision model configured, the extraction pipeline runs in the background
and the status walks forward through its stages. Without one — the
default on every install — the receipt goes straight to `COMPLETE` with
`reviewRequired: true` and the member fills the fields in through
`PATCH /v1/receipts/{id}`. That is the ordinary outcome, not an error,
and it is never a 4xx.

item.name: Subscribe a URL to this member's events

description.content:
Registers an HTTPS endpoint this server will POST to when one of the
caller's subscribed events happens.

**`targetUrl` is checked by the shared egress policy, and it is checked
again on every delivery attempt.** A refusal here is 400
`outbound-url-rejected` with a sentence naming the rule — the scheme,
or the address range the host resolves to — but never the resolved
address itself, which would turn this route into an internal port
scanner. Re-checking at delivery time is what closes the DNS-rebinding
window: a name that answers a public address while you are saving it
and a private one an hour later is refused at the second point, and the
HTTP client connects to the address the policy approved rather than
resolving the name a second time of its own accord.

**`secret` is write-only.** It is encrypted at rest with the same
AES-GCM field encryption the AI API key and the SimpleFIN access URL
use, it appears in no response schema, and it is never logged. Every
delivery carries `X-Trove-Signature: sha256=<hex>`, an HMAC-SHA256 over
the exact request bytes keyed with it, alongside `X-Trove-Event` (the
event type) and `X-Trove-Delivery` (the delivery id, stable across
retries so a receiver can deduplicate).

Deliveries are retried with exponential backoff — 2^n seconds, five
attempts — and a subscription that never succeeds is left `EXHAUSTED`
rather than retried for ever.

A member may hold at most twenty subscriptions
(`trove.notifications.max-webhooks-per-user`); the twenty-first is 409
`conflict`. Every subscription is an outbound connection this server
makes on that member's behalf, so the number is capped rather than
unbounded.
